main.title: Culdcept Saga
main.subtitle: A deck becomes the means of travelling a board
main.summary: Culdcept Saga is OmiyaSoft and Jamsworks' Xbox 360 strategy game, first released in Japan on 22 November 2006. It combines a board-game route with collectible cards, allowing creatures, equipment and spells to affect the contest over territory. The story follows a young man whose unexpected affinity with magical cards draws him into a larger journey. Every match asks the player to connect a prepared deck to the opportunities that appear on the board. A useful card is not valuable in isolation; it must answer the position and resources available when the turn arrives.

cards.heading: A deck becomes the means of travelling a board
cards.text: Culdcept Saga is OmiyaSoft and Jamsworks' Xbox 360 strategy game, first released in Japan on 22 November 2006. It combines a board-game route with collectible cards, allowing creatures, equipment and spells to affect the contest over territory. The story follows a young man whose unexpected affinity with magical cards draws him into a larger journey. Every match asks the player to connect a prepared deck to the opportunities that appear on the board. A useful card is not valuable in isolation; it must answer the position and resources available when the turn arrives.

cards.heading: Prepare a plan that can survive a different draw
cards.text: Creatures claim and defend spaces, while equipment and spells change the result of confrontations or the wider state of play. The cards available at a particular moment limit what can be attempted, so the deck needs to offer several useful responses rather than depend on one ideal sequence. Moving around the board introduces another layer of opportunity and risk. The player reads both systems together, deciding which territory is worth contesting and which resource should be saved. Strategy develops through adapting the intended plan to the cards actually drawn.

cards.heading: An unusual strategy series reaches Xbox
cards.text: Artist Midori Harada and writer Tow Ubukata contributed to the production, with Kenji Ito composing the music. Culdcept Saga became the series' first release for a Microsoft console. The North American edition arrived in February 2008, more than a year after Japan, while Europe and Australia did not receive an original release. Multiplayer gives the board-and-card combination a different character when other people are choosing the risks. Its appeal lies in that mixture: the board establishes where the contest takes place, but the deck can repeatedly change what a position means.

main.title: Jeanne d'Arc
main.subtitle: A familiar history becomes a fantasy
main.summary: Jeanne d'Arc is Level-5's tactical role-playing game for PSP, first released in Japan on 22 November 2006. Its Joan of Arc inhabits a fantasy version of the Hundred Years' War, where magical powers and monsters accompany the struggle against English forces. Jeanne gathers companions and leads them across a succession of battlefields. The historical outline supplies names and a direction for the journey, while the supernatural elements give its combat another set of possibilities. Animated sequences and expressive characters introduce a campaign designed around battles fought one decision at a time.

cards.heading: A familiar history becomes a fantasy
cards.text: Jeanne d'Arc is Level-5's tactical role-playing game for PSP, first released in Japan on 22 November 2006. Its Joan of Arc inhabits a fantasy version of the Hundred Years' War, where magical powers and monsters accompany the struggle against English forces. Jeanne gathers companions and leads them across a succession of battlefields. The historical outline supplies names and a direction for the journey, while the supernatural elements give its combat another set of possibilities. Animated sequences and expressive characters introduce a campaign designed around battles fought one decision at a time.

cards.heading: Make the position help the next attack
cards.text: Battles take place on a grid, with each member of the party moving and acting in turn. Weapon reach, surrounding allies and the direction of an approach affect what can be achieved from one square. Special skills offer attacks and recovery beyond the basic options, giving each character another role to develop. The player must consider the group rather than only Jeanne: leaving one fighter isolated can make the next enemy turn dangerous, while a careful formation creates opportunities for several companions to support the same advance.

cards.heading: Power carried in a bracelet
cards.text: Magical armlets allow certain characters to transform, temporarily gaining strength and additional abilities. Choosing when to use that advantage becomes part of managing a difficult encounter. Skill gems can be equipped and combined, letting the party's development continue between battles. Ken Motomura directed Level-5's first tactical role-playing game and its first PSP production, with Takeshi Inoue composing the music. The original release reached North America in 2007. Its later PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 edition in 2024 also brought the adventure to European audiences for the first time.

main.title: Garry's Mod
main.summary: Garry's Mod, commonly clipped as GMod, is a 2006 sandbox game developed by Facepunch Studios and published by Valve.

cards.heading: A sandbox without a fixed objective
cards.text: Garry's Mod, commonly clipped as GMod, is a 2006 sandbox game developed by Facepunch Studios and published by Valve. The base game mode of Garry's Mod has no set objectives and provides the player with a world in which to freely manipulate objects. Other game modes, notably Trouble in Terrorist Town and Prop Hunt, are created by other developers as mods and are installed separately, by means such as the Steam Workshop.

cards.heading: From a Source mod to a standalone game
cards.text: Garry's Mod was created by Garry Newman as a mod for Valve's Source game engine and released in December 2004, before being expanded into a standalone release that was published by Valve in November 2006. Ports of the original Windows version for Mac OS X and Linux followed in September 2010 and June 2013, respectively. As of September 2021, Garry's Mod has sold more than 20 million copies. A spiritual successor, S&box, was released in 2026.

main.title: WarioWare: Smooth Moves
main.subtitle: A new pose before every game
main.summary: WarioWare: Smooth Moves is Nintendo and Intelligent Systems' Wii collection of very short games built around different ways of holding the Wii Remote. Wario and the other inhabitants of Diamond City introduce stages in which a simple instruction must be understood and performed within seconds. The controller may become an umbrella, a handle or something held against the body. Each new pose prepares the next joke and the next action, making the player's changing posture part of the spectacle as much as the images appearing on the television.

cards.heading: A new pose before every game
cards.text: WarioWare: Smooth Moves is Nintendo and Intelligent Systems' Wii collection of very short games built around different ways of holding the Wii Remote. Wario and the other inhabitants of Diamond City introduce stages in which a simple instruction must be understood and performed within seconds. The controller may become an umbrella, a handle or something held against the body. Each new pose prepares the next joke and the next action, making the player's changing posture part of the spectacle as much as the images appearing on the television.

cards.heading: Understand the instruction before time runs out
cards.text: Before a microgame begins, an illustration demonstrates how to hold the Remote. The following prompt then asks for a brief movement or decision using that position. Failing costs one of the stage's lives, while a sequence of successful actions leads toward a longer boss challenge. The format leaves little time for explanation, relying on recognisable objects and readable motions. A player learns to connect the suggested pose with the immediate situation, turning a few seconds of confusion into the satisfaction of understanding what the game expects.

cards.heading: The controller passes around the room
cards.text: Completing the single-player stages opens multiplayer activities in which one Wii Remote can be shared by a group of up to twelve. Watching another person perform an unusual pose becomes part of the entertainment before the controller reaches the next player. The arrangement gives a rapid succession of small games a social rhythm beyond the screen. Smooth Moves uses the Wii's motion controls as a source of physical comedy, making the act of discovering how to hold the controller inseparable from discovering how to play the next game.

main.title: Wii Play
main.summary: Wii Play is a 2006 party video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii.

cards.text: Wii Play is a 2006 party video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii. It was released as a launch game for the console in Japan, Europe, and Australia in December 2006, and was released in North America in February 2007. The game features nine minigames, including a Duck Hunt-esque shooting range, a fishing game, and a billiards game, each of which are designed to showcase the features of the Wii Remote controller.

Developed as a compilation of prototype games originally shown off at E3 2006, Wii Play was developed by Nintendo EAD simultaneously with Wii Sports, which also contained tech demos from E3. The featured games make use of several aspects of the Wii Remote, such as its detection of rotation and depth movement through motion sensing and its infrared pointer.

Wii Play sold 28.02 million copies worldwide, helped by its inclusion with an additional Wii Remote. Critics were less enthusiastic about the repetitive minigames. The package nevertheless gave new owners a controller and a set of short activities for learning its features. Nintendo followed it with Wii Play: Motion in 2011.

main.title: Metal Gear Solid: Portable Ops
main.summary: Metal Gear Solid: Portable Ops, officially abbreviated MPO, is a 2006 action-adventure stealth game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation Portable.

cards.heading: A PSP mission for Naked Snake
cards.text: Metal Gear Solid: Portable Ops, officially abbreviated MPO, is a 2006 action-adventure stealth game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation Portable. The game was directed by Masahiro Yamamoto and written by Gakuto Mikumo, with series creator Hideo Kojima acting as producer.

cards.heading: Captured by the renegade FOX unit
cards.text: Portable Ops carries the main series' action-based stealth onto PSP after the Metal Gear Acid games and Digital Graphic Novel. Set in 1970, six years after Snake Eater, it begins with Naked Snake captured in Colombia by the renegade FOX unit. Escaping and recruiting allies become the basis of his response.

cards.heading: Preparing a four-person squad
cards.text: The Comrade System asks the player to assemble a four-person squad before each mission. Members have different strengths: some excel in a fight, while others contribute to item production, healing or intelligence. The game also draws on Snake Eater and uses the camera approach of its Subsistence edition. Choosing who to take and how to use them adds preparation to the familiar infiltration.

cards.heading: Switching the soldier in play
cards.text: During missions, the player controls only one squad member at a time. Squad members not in use will hide themselves inside a cardboard box, and can be swapped into play when the player-controlled character finds a hiding spot, where he or she will hide in a cardboard box.

cards.heading: Recruiting enemies and finding new allies
cards.text: Stunning or tranquilising an enemy allows the player to drag them to a vehicle for recruitment. An ally waiting in a cardboard box can transport the captive, saving Snake's stamina. New personnel can also be found through Wi-Fi access points and the PSP GPS Receiver. Recruits include soldiers, scientists, engineers and officers. A generic soldier can pass among similar personnel if the player avoids suspicious actions, making the choice of recruit useful during infiltration.

cards.heading: The cost of losing a squad member
cards.text: Characters who are killed in combat are eliminated from the player's squad permanently. "Unique characters" (i.e. characters important to the game's story, who can only be added into the player's squad by fulfilling certain tasks) are exempt from this rule. If a unique character is wounded in combat, they are sent to an infirmary to recover, making them unusable for a few in-game days. The player can also restart or abort a mission at any moment.

cards.heading: Reading sounds on the surround indicator
cards.text: Another new feature is the surround indicator added to the game's HUD. Similar to the radar in previous titles, the surround indicator allows players to determine the relative proximity of enemy soldiers by the noises they make. The surround indicator is composed of two circles; the outer circle displays the noises made by enemies and the inner circle displays noises made by the player's character.

main.title: Blue Dragon
main.subtitle: Five young travellers and the creatures in their shadows
main.summary: Blue Dragon first reached Xbox 360 in Japan on December 7, 2006. Mistwalker and Artoon brought together Hironobu Sakaguchi’s role-playing direction, Akira Toriyama’s character designs and Nobuo Uematsu’s music. Shu and his companions confront Nene’s machines with creatures that emerge from their own shadows: a dragon, a phoenix and other powerful silhouettes turn ordinary gestures into spectacular attacks. The colourful adventure places its young travellers among villages, ancient technology and the remains of a vanished civilisation.

cards.heading: A dragon at your heels
cards.text: Blue Dragon first reached Xbox 360 in Japan on December 7, 2006. Mistwalker and Artoon brought together Hironobu Sakaguchi’s role-playing direction, Akira Toriyama’s character designs and Nobuo Uematsu’s music. Shu and his companions confront Nene’s machines with creatures that emerge from their own shadows: a dragon, a phoenix and other powerful silhouettes turn ordinary gestures into spectacular attacks. The colourful adventure places its young travellers among villages, ancient technology and the remains of a vanished civilisation.

cards.heading: Choosing what a shadow can become
cards.text: The battles are turn-based, but the party’s abilities are not fixed by its character designs. Changing a shadow’s class changes its role, and equipping learned skills gives the player room to shape a fighter, healer or support specialist. Enemies can be seen while exploring; the Encounter Circle lets the player select nearby opponents, while consecutive fights can bring bonuses. Uematsu’s score moves between gentle melodies and the striking boss song Eternity, sung by Ian Gillan. The original Xbox 360 game later joined Xbox One backward compatibility and became available digitally in 2016.

main.title: Yakuza 2
main.subtitle: Two dragons in the same country
main.summary: Yakuza 2 is Sega's PlayStation 2 action-adventure, first released in Japan on 7 December 2006. Kazuma Kiryu returns to help the Tojo Clan as its relationship with the Omi Alliance threatens to become a war. His opponent Ryuji Goda, known as the Dragon of Kansai, gives the conflict a rival with a clear presence. The story moves between Kamurocho and Osaka's Sotenbori, combining organised crime, personal history and street fighting. Western releases followed in 2008, retaining the original Japanese voices with translated text.

cards.heading: Two dragons in the same country
cards.text: Yakuza 2 is Sega's PlayStation 2 action-adventure, first released in Japan on 7 December 2006. Kazuma Kiryu returns to help the Tojo Clan as its relationship with the Omi Alliance threatens to become a war. His opponent Ryuji Goda, known as the Dragon of Kansai, gives the conflict a rival with a clear presence. The story moves between Kamurocho and Osaka's Sotenbori, combining organised crime, personal history and street fighting. Western releases followed in 2008, retaining the original Japanese voices with translated text.

cards.heading: A city between the fights
cards.text: Kiryu explores busy urban districts, talks to residents and becomes involved in side stories before returning to the main conflict. Shops, restaurants and recreational activities make the streets useful places to spend time rather than corridors between battles. Encounters break into close-range fights where the player combines attacks and uses objects found nearby. Improvements to the fighting system build on the first game's approach. Moving between an urgent crime drama and a stranger, smaller encounter gives the city a rhythm beyond the central plot.

cards.heading: A conflict with a personal history
cards.text: Detective Kaoru Sayama's investigation brings another perspective to Kiryu's return, while the story connects present alliances to events from the past. The rivalry with Ryuji sits within those relationships rather than replacing them. Directed by Ryuta Ueda, the sequel expanded the locations and activities established by Yakuza. Its later HD editions preserved the original adventure, and Yakuza Kiwami 2 rebuilt it with newer technology in 2017. The PlayStation 2 release marks the point where Kiryu's story grew beyond a single district and its first crisis.

main.title: MotorStorm
main.subtitle: A route for every machine
main.summary: MotorStorm is Evolution Studios' off-road racer for PlayStation 3, first released in Japan in December 2006. A festival in Monument Valley brings motorcycles, buggies, rally cars and heavy trucks into the same races. Their different strengths make choosing a vehicle part of choosing a route through the desert.

cards.heading: Into the same race
cards.text: MotorStorm is Evolution Studios' off-road racer for PlayStation 3, first released in Japan in December 2006. A festival in Monument Valley brings motorcycles, buggies, rally cars and heavy trucks into the same races. Their different strengths make choosing a vehicle part of choosing a route through the desert.

cards.heading: Weight against agility
cards.text: A bike can use a narrow opening that leaves a larger machine struggling, but its rider has little protection when the field closes around it. A big rig brings weight and a different response to rough ground. Those differences remain visible throughout a race. Passing another vehicle can mean finding a route it handles poorly, while entering its preferred ground gives the advantage back.

cards.heading: Learning several routes
cards.text: The tracks divide into paths at different heights, with ramps, drops and muddy sections changing what a corner asks of each class. A line that looks direct from one vehicle can be expensive from another. The designers built those routes around the competing machines, so learning a track involves returning to familiar ground with a different set of strengths and limitations.

cards.heading: Knowing when to cool down
cards.text: Boost gives every vehicle a short-term increase in speed, but sustained use heats the engine towards an explosion. Letting it cool before a difficult section can be more useful than spending it on the first open straight. The gauge makes that decision immediate: another second might secure a pass, or leave the vehicle in pieces before the corner. Speed depends on judging how much the machine can still give.

main.title: Dragon Quest Monsters: Joker
main.subtitle: Recruit the monsters that usually block the road
main.summary: Dragon Quest Monsters: Joker is Tose's Nintendo DS role-playing game following a young scout who recruits familiar Dragon Quest creatures to fight on his behalf. Travelling between the islands of Green Bays supplies the encounters needed to build a team for the monster-scouting competition. The subseries moves into three-dimensional surroundings, with monsters visible in the landscape before battle begins. Its central pleasure is developing the creatures normally met as opponents, turning a new encounter into the possibility of another companion and another way to arrange the next fight.

cards.heading: Recruit the monsters that usually block the road
cards.text: Dragon Quest Monsters: Joker is Tose's Nintendo DS role-playing game following a young scout who recruits familiar Dragon Quest creatures to fight on his behalf. Travelling between the islands of Green Bays supplies the encounters needed to build a team for the monster-scouting competition. The subseries moves into three-dimensional surroundings, with monsters visible in the landscape before battle begins. Its central pleasure is developing the creatures normally met as opponents, turning a new encounter into the possibility of another companion and another way to arrange the next fight.

cards.heading: Three companions take the field
cards.text: A battle party contains up to three monsters, which can receive direct commands or follow selected tactics. The human scout supports the group with items rather than joining the attacks. Monsters encountered in the landscape can be avoided or approached, and attacking from behind can provide an early advantage. The visible encounters give exploration a practical choice before the turn-based system takes over. A player can seek a particular creature, prepare for the meeting or continue toward another destination instead of accepting every battle as an unseen interruption.

cards.heading: The next island offers another possibility
cards.text: Jet-ski routes connect the main islands, with occasional uncharted destinations adding another reason to pay attention during travel. Building a useful collection gives those excursions a purpose beyond simply following the tournament route. The original online system also allowed a team to be ranked and matched against downloaded opponents, extending the test beyond the main adventure. Joker connects exploration with preparation through these different encounters: what is found while travelling becomes part of a team whose strengths can then be tested in another setting against a different arrangement of monsters.
